sections.h2: Where is Woburn, and what kind of place is it?
sections.html:
Woburn is a city in Middlesex County, Massachusetts, about 9 miles north of Boston. It covers roughly 12.9 square miles and shares borders with Wilmington, Reading, Stoneham, Winchester, Lexington and Burlington.

The 2020 census counted 40,876 residents living in 16,590 households, with 17,540 housing units, about 5.4% of them vacant at the time. The median age was 40.8. Woburn runs on a mayor and city council, and it was the last Massachusetts municipality to stop calling council members aldermen.

Woburn sits at about 98 feet of elevation, and Horn Pond, where the town was first settled, is a primary source of the Mystic River. For a seller, the practical point is that a buyer can compare your house with others in a city of roughly 44,000 people, which the Census Bureau estimated at 43,962 in July 2025.

sections.h2: How much of Woburn's history is still visible in its houses?
sections.html:
A good deal of it is. Woburn was first settled in 1640 near Horn Pond and became a town in 1642. Its territory once included what are now Winchester, Burlington and parts of Stoneham and Wilmington, which split off over the next two centuries.

The city grew around tanning and transport. A tannery was built in 1668, the Middlesex Canal opened in 1803, and the Boston and Lowell Railroad began running through town in 1835. Route 128 opened in 1951 and Route 93 came through in 1963, which pulled the city toward Boston commuters and offices.

  • Several 18th and 19th century houses survive, including the 1790 House and the Baldwin House beside a stretch of the old canal.
  • The population jumped from about 20,500 in 1950 to 31,200 in 1960 and 37,400 in 1970, so a large share of the housing dates from those postwar decades.

If your house is one of the older ones, a cash buyer prices the age and condition into the offer directly instead of asking you to fix things first.

Woburn has a mixed economy of retail, healthcare, manufacturing and office parks. Companies headquartered here include Boston Acoustics, Monotype and Skyworks Solutions. Cummings Properties, a large commercial landlord in the region, was founded in Woburn in 1970.

The state labor department's list of top employers, as reproduced on Wikipedia, groups Woburn employers by headcount band:

Courts and county offices add to the daytime population. The Middlesex Superior Court moved to the TradeCenter 128 campus in 2008, and the Probate and Family Court and the county sheriff's office followed in 2020 and 2022. The Registry of Deeds is the one county office that stayed in Cambridge, so ask your closing attorney or title company where the deed will be recorded.

sections.h2: What should a seller know about Woburn's water and groundwater history?
sections.html:
Woburn is one of the few communities near Boston that supplies its own drinking water. According to Wikipedia, the supply comes mostly from five wells in the Horn Pond aquifer, treated at the Horn Pond Treatment Plant, with about a third supplemented by the Massachusetts Water Resources Authority.

The city also carries a well-known environmental history. In 1979, high levels of chemical contamination were found in city Wells G and H, and families in the Pine Street area of east Woburn raised concerns about childhood leukemia. A lawsuit followed in 1982, and the story became the book and film titled A Civil Action.

That history is decades old, and we are not saying any particular street is affected today. It does explain why buyers and their lenders in Woburn sometimes ask about environmental questions on older industrial or neighboring parcels. If your house sits near former industrial land, ask the city's Water Department and the Massachusetts Department of Environmental Protection what records exist, and tell any buyer what you learn.

sections.h2: How do people get around, and does it affect value?
sections.html:
Woburn is split between two highway corridors and one rail hub. Route 128 and Route 93 both pass through, and the Anderson Regional Transportation Center is the main transit stop.

  • MBTA Commuter Rail to Boston's North Station and to Lowell.
  • Amtrak service to Portland, Maine.
  • Bus service to Logan International Airport and Manchester-Boston Regional Airport.
  • MBTA bus routes along Main Street, Montvale Avenue, Lexington Street and Cambridge Road.

The older Mishawum commuter rail stop stopped service on December 14, 2020. Location near the station or highway ramps is one of the first things a buyer will weigh, and it is worth mentioning when you describe your house to us.

Woburn Public Schools runs seven elementary schools: Goodyear, Altavesta, Shamrock, Malcolm White, Reeves, Linscott-Rumford and Hurld-Wyman. Students then move to the John F. Kennedy or Daniel L. Joyce middle school and on to Woburn Memorial High School. Northeast Metro Tech serves as the vocational school, and St. Charles is a private Catholic school for kindergarten through eighth grade.

Several former school buildings, including Clapp, Plympton and Wyman, have been closed or repurposed. We do not publish school ratings here, since we have not confirmed a current official figure.

sections.h2: What does it cost to hold a Woburn house while you sell?
sections.html:
Property tax is the main carrying cost, and Woburn publishes its residential rate history on the Assessing Department page. The rates below are per $1,000 of assessed value, as listed by the city:

Fiscal yearResidentialCommercial, industrial, personal
2026$9.15$21.43
2025$8.54$20.41
2024$8.06$19.72
2023$8.70$21.14
2022$9.34$22.77

The Assessing Department is on the second floor of City Hall at 10 Common Street. The chief appraiser is John Connolly, and the phone is 781-897-5830. The office handles exemptions for elderly, widowed, blind and disabled veteran owners and posts a homestead page and an abutters list request form. The city also announced cyclical property inspections running from May to November 2026, so a visit from an assessor is possible.

For the rules that apply across the state, see our Massachusetts property tax guide.

sections.h2: What steps does a Woburn sale involve?
sections.html:
A Woburn sale follows Massachusetts law, plus a few local contacts. Three items come up most often.

  • Smoke detectors. Under M.G.L. c. 148, section 26F, a residential building must be equipped by the seller with approved smoke detectors when it is sold or transferred, and the head of the fire department enforces it. Call the Woburn Fire Department to schedule the inspection.
  • Deed excise tax. M.G.L. c. 64D, section 1 sets the excise at $2 for each $500 of consideration, or fraction of it. Your closing attorney will confirm who pays and in what amount.
  • Tax proration. Unpaid or current tax is settled at closing, typically from the seller's proceeds.

These are the same steps whether you list, sell by owner or take a cash offer. What changes is how long they take and how many contingencies surround them.

sections.h2: How does selling to a cash buyer work in Woburn?
sections.html:
Selling for cash in Woburn means a buyer purchases the house as it stands, without a mortgage contingency. We look at the address, the condition and any liens or taxes, then present an offer. If you accept, a title company or attorney handles the paperwork and the closing date is set around your timeline.

That path can fit a Woburn owner who inherited an older house, who owns a two or three family with a difficult tenant, or who simply does not want to repaint, replace a heating system and hold open houses. You can also turn the offer down and keep your options open.

If you are unsure whether to list or sell as is, call or text us and we will walk through both with you, with no pressure to choose.

faqs.q: How far is Woburn from Boston?
faqs.a: Woburn sits about 9 miles north of Boston in Middlesex County. Route 128 and Route 93 both run through the city, and the Anderson Regional Transportation Center offers commuter rail to North Station.

faqs.q: Do I need a smoke detector inspection to sell my Woburn house?
faqs.a: Yes. Massachusetts law requires the seller to equip a residential building with approved smoke detectors on sale or transfer, and the head of the fire department enforces it. Contact the Woburn Fire Department to arrange it before closing.

faqs.q: What is the Woburn residential property tax rate?
faqs.a: The city lists $9.15 per $1,000 of assessed value for fiscal year 2026, up from $8.54 in fiscal year 2025. Check the Assessing Department page for the current figure before you rely on it.

faqs.q: Where are deeds recorded for a Woburn sale?
faqs.a: Woburn is in Middlesex County, and the county's Registry of Deeds remained in Cambridge even after many other county offices moved to Woburn. Your closing attorney or title company records the deed there.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Woburn house that has repairs or tenants?
faqs.a: Yes. A cash buyer purchases as is, so a roof, heating or tenant issue does not have to be solved first. Ask your closing attorney about notice rules if tenants live in the house.

faqs.q: Whom do I ask about taxes on a Woburn house?
faqs.a: Start with the Woburn Assessing Department at 10 Common Street, second floor of City Hall, or call 781-897-5830. For anything this page does not cover, ask the office directly.
